post1.text:
Scaling a company doesn't fail because of bad strategy. It fails because leadership doesn't scale with it.

Most founders and CEOs who built a $50M business did it by being everywhere, deciding everything, and trusting almost no one. That exact behavior becomes the ceiling at $100M, $200M, and beyond.

Recent news confirms the pattern: companies that successfully push into new markets and larger infrastructure aren't just hiring more people. They're restructuring how leadership itself operates. The executive team expands not to add headcount, but to distribute judgment.

Here's what that actually looks like in practice:

1. The CEO stops being the best decision-maker in the room and starts being the person who builds rooms full of better ones.
2. Leadership capacity gets planned 18 months ahead of revenue targets, not in reaction to them.
3. Culture stops being a feeling and starts being a system with owners.

The question most leaders never ask themselves: Is the person running your company today capable of running the company you're trying to build tomorrow?

post2.text:
A recent piece in citybiz covered how Strive Health expanded its executive team specifically to scale its value-based kidney care model. What caught our attention wasn't the hiring news. It was the reason behind it.

They didn't grow the leadership team after hitting a new revenue milestone. They grew it to get there.

That distinction matters enormously for companies in the $50M to $500M range. At that stage, most organizations are still running on the leadership structure that got them to $50M. That structure wasn't built to carry them further.

At Autobahn, we see this consistently: the companies that scale successfully treat leadership capacity as a growth lever, not an org chart update.

If your executive team looks the same as it did two years ago, it might be time to ask whether it's built for where you're going.

post3.text:
Every week we see another announcement about a growing company strengthening its executive team to hit the next level. It's the right move. But most leaders don't know what they're actually building when they do it.

Chapter 1 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, is titled Lead Like Lives Depend On It. Written by Katherine Slain, this chapter confronts something most leadership books won't say directly: the leadership identity that made you successful at $50M is not the one that will carry you to $500M.

Katherine doesn't just describe the gap. She gives leaders a way to see themselves clearly enough to close it, before the company pays the price for the delay.

This is the chapter we wish more executives read before they needed it.

post1.text:
Most business owners think about their exit six months too late. By then, the multiple is already set.

Here is the uncomfortable truth: your valuation is not determined at the negotiating table. It is built over years of decisions that either compress or expand what a buyer is willing to pay. J.P. Morgan's private banking guidance on exit strategies reinforces this point directly. The owners who command premium multiples are the ones who treated their exit as a design problem, not a timing problem.

Three things that actually move the needle for $50M+ companies:

1. Revenue quality matters more than revenue size. Recurring, predictable income streams are valued at a significant premium over one-time project revenue.

2. Customer concentration is a silent multiple killer. If one client represents more than 15% of your revenue, buyers discount accordingly.

3. Leadership depth signals enterprise value. If the business cannot operate without the founder, buyers are not buying a company. They are buying a job.

What is the one thing in your business that a sophisticated buyer would flag on day one of due diligence?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Silicon Valley Bank on exit strategies raises a question that more midmarket leaders need to sit with: when is the wrong time to sell, even when buyers are circling?

SVB's perspective is useful, but here is what we see working with companies scaling from $50M to $500M and beyond: the decision to sell is rarely just financial. It is operational. Leaders who have not stress-tested their business model, cleaned up their cap table, or built a management team that runs without them almost always leave money on the table, regardless of market conditions.

Timing the market is far less valuable than timing your readiness. If you are evaluating an exit in the next two to five years, the work starts now.

Read the full SVB piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMinwFBVV95cUxQeXI2ZzYxYnJkdGhyZ1FlaVBlWXQ1RjB4ZnhCRWtFVEpBZ0FPZnB4amFmV2xxVmxJbXRMR0dfeHlmWkw2V0syR3pfdGdMaGJvMDVPQ1FYZUgwaU1wcnRFVkU0aExWQ01yQUJFQTd3Z0NrZG9sR3Q3XzQ5cF9IZEJuWDdsNmZ5dUJjVjZ3NEZqQ2preC1henhFRnV6MWtXRWc

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce recently outlined the core elements of building an exit strategy. Good foundation. But for companies operating at $50M and above, the stakes demand a sharper framework.

Chapter 2 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, is titled 'Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit.' Chapter authors Paul Belair and George Hohman work with owners at this level every day, and they are direct about something most advisors avoid: not all revenue, growth, or profit is valued equally by acquirers.

The chapter unpacks how buyers actually calculate risk into your multiple, and what levers you can pull right now to change that calculus before you ever sit across from an LOI.

If you are building toward an exit, this chapter alone is worth the read.

post1.text:
Most strategic plans fail not because the strategy was wrong, but because leadership never agreed on what execution actually looks like.

Forbes recently explored why leadership teams break down at the execution stage, and the core finding is uncomfortable: the problem is almost never the plan. It is the people at the top who cannot align on priorities, accountability, or what done means.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, this is where growth stalls. Here is what that looks like in practice:

1. Strategy gets written in a room and forgotten in the field. The gap between the deck and daily decisions is where momentum dies.

2. Accountability without clarity is just pressure. Leaders need to know not just what they own, but how success gets measured at every level.

3. Execution is a rhythm, not a moment. Companies that scale treat strategy review as an operating discipline, not an annual event.

So here is the real question: Does your leadership team have a shared definition of what it means to win this year?

#StrategicPlanning #BusinessGrowth #ExecutionExcellence

post2.text:
A recent piece from Harvard Business School Online tackled one of the most persistent problems in growing companies: getting employees to actually believe in and act on strategic initiatives.

The findings are worth paying attention to if you are scaling past $50M. At that stage, your strategy stops being a leadership conversation and starts being an organizational behavior problem. You can have the right plan and still watch it dissolve because the people responsible for carrying it out were never brought in.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly. Leaders assume communication equals buy-in. It does not. Buy-in requires involvement, context, and a clear line between what employees are being asked to do and why it matters to the business.

If your team is executing against a strategy they do not understand or believe in, the plan is already broken.

Read the full piece and think honestly about where your gaps are.

post3.text:
Employee buy-in. Strategic alignment. Execution that actually holds. These are not soft concepts. They are the difference between a company that grows and one that grinds.

In Chapter 3 of Rock Your Business, titled 'What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes,' authors Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall draw on real experience across wildly different industries to show what strategic planning looks like when it is built to survive contact with reality.

One thing they make clear: the businesses that scale are not the ones with the most sophisticated plans. They are the ones where leaders learned to translate strategy into decisions people could actually make on the floor, in the store, and in the field.

The framework they share is practical, field-tested, and built for companies that cannot afford to get this wrong.

post1.text:
Most companies at $50M don't have a sales strategy. They have a collection of habits that worked once.

There's a difference. And it's costing them more than they realize.

Bain & Company recently studied what separates B2B companies that consistently win new customers from those that plateau. The answer wasn't a better product or a bigger team. It was a repeatable, structured approach to capturing demand, one that most mid-market firms have never actually built.

Here's what that means in practice:

First, random acts of selling are not a strategy. If your top rep leaving would crater your pipeline, you don't have a system.

Second, growth at this stage requires separating who you're targeting from how you're reaching them. Conflating the two creates noise, not revenue.

Third, the companies that scale past $200M almost always have a defined sales motion before they need it, not after.

If your revenue is growing but your close rate isn't, what does that tell you about where the real problem actually lives?

post2.text:
A recent piece in McKinsey and Company on the economics of B2B growth raised a number that should stop every mid-market CEO cold: the revenue threshold required just to survive competitively has shifted significantly upward. Standing still is no longer neutral. It is decline.

At Autobahn, we see this play out constantly with companies in the $50M to $200M range. Leaders assume their current sales approach will carry them to the next level because it got them here. It won't.

What McKinsey is describing is exactly why a real, documented sales strategy is not optional at this stage. It is the difference between scaling and stalling.

Read the full piece and think about where your sales motion would hold up under pressure.

post3.text:
WSJ recently outlined four commerce strategies helping B2B companies drive new revenue. Good list. But here is the part most articles skip: none of those strategies work without the foundation underneath them.

Chapter 4 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, is titled Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation. Authors Deb and Brandon lay out why companies at the $50M mark are often the most vulnerable, not because business is bad, but because the sales approach that produced early success quietly becomes the ceiling that blocks what comes next.

One of the sharpest insights in the chapter: most leadership teams can describe their sales results, but very few can describe their sales system. Those are not the same thing, and the gap between them is expensive.

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is the feeling people get when they interact with your company, and most $50M+ leaders have no idea what that feeling actually is.

Campari has managed some of the world's most recognizable spirits brands for decades by staying ruthlessly connected to cultural relevance without abandoning their heritage. That balance is not accidental. It is a deliberate strategic choice made at the leadership level.

Here is what scaling companies miss:

1. Brand is a business asset, not a marketing expense. If your CFO cannot connect brand investment to revenue retention, you have a measurement problem.

2. Consistency beats creativity. A brand that shows up differently in sales, marketing, and customer success is not a brand. It is noise.

3. Culture and brand are the same thing facing different directions. One faces inward. One faces out. They had better match.

If a stranger walked into your best customer's office tomorrow and asked what your company stands for, what would they say?

#Branding #BusinessGrowth #ScalingUp

post2.text:
A recent piece in Marketing Dive on Ulta's CMO caught our attention here at Autobahn Consultants.

The conversation around blending brand building with omnichannel marketing is exactly where companies scaling past $50M tend to struggle. At that size, you have enough channels to create real confusion and not yet enough infrastructure to manage them well.

Ulta's approach reinforces something we see in our best-performing clients: brand is not a campaign. It is an operating system. Your messaging, your customer experience, your sales motion, all of it has to run on the same code.

If your marketing feels inconsistent across touchpoints, that is a strategy problem, not a creative one. The fix starts at the leadership level, not in the marketing department.

Read the full piece and think about where your own brand breaks down across channels.

post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a cost.

Most companies scaling past $50M default to headcount as the answer to every operational problem. More revenue pressure? Hire. More complexity? Hire. The result is a bloated org that moves slower than it did at half the size.

SHRM's latest research on 2026 hiring trends makes this clear: the companies winning on talent right now are not the ones casting the widest nets. They are the ones getting surgical. They know exactly which roles drive disproportionate value and they hire with that precision in mind.

Here is what that looks like in practice for a scaling business:

1. Define the 20% of roles responsible for 80% of your revenue outcomes before you post a single job.
2. Build scorecards around those roles, not generic job descriptions.
3. Treat every hire above $100M revenue as a structural decision, not just a people decision.

Most leadership teams optimize for speed to hire. The ones who scale cleanly optimize for cost of a wrong hire.

What is the last role you filled that you wish you had thought harder about before posting it?

post2.text:
A recent piece on the Workday Blog digs into how agentic AI is reshaping talent acquisition, with automation now handling sourcing, screening, and candidate engagement at a scale no recruiting team could match manually.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, this is not a future-state conversation. It is a right-now competitive pressure.

Here is Autobahn's take: technology does not fix a broken talent process. It accelerates it. Before any scaling company invests in AI-driven hiring tools, the leadership team needs to know exactly what a great hire looks like in each critical role. Without that clarity, faster sourcing just means faster bad decisions.

The companies who will win with these tools are the ones who already have the human judgment locked in. The tools just execute it faster.

Read the full piece and think about where your process ends and the tool begins: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMihwFBVV95cUxQWEx1eXkyai1wcUgzZnZsUkNGSTVmLWV6eTVhWGo5TG5Nem9CUE1neW54UlFCbldsbVZzQnIwZ0lYUXFLSUx2NFNlM3VOY2Y0QlpxRk9aSnJBZ2tNY3Y0MEpaZmw5VDZVM3VJRlo4WjNyd2VSZ0pTQnY4VFduMTZvdlFOZVlBdlE

post3.text:
SHRM's recent piece on precision hiring in 2026 lands on something Chapter 6 of Rock Your Business confronts head-on.

The chapter is called The Talent Engine. Authors Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West wrote it for one reason: most companies scaling past $50M are building their people strategy on instinct instead of infrastructure.

One of the sharpest insights in the chapter is that talent problems at scale are almost never recruiting problems. They are clarity problems. Leaders who cannot articulate what great looks like in a role will not recognize it when it walks through the door, no matter how sophisticated their hiring process becomes.

The chapter gives you a framework for building a talent engine that does not depend on any single leader's gut. That distinction matters more than most executives realize until it is too late.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not make better decisions. They make slower ones.

Most leadership teams at the $50M+ level are not suffering from a lack of data. They are drowning in it. Oracle NetSuite recently published a list of 30 financial metrics businesses should track heading into 2026. The list is thorough. It is also a warning sign if your team feels compelled to monitor all of them.

Here is what high-performing scaling companies actually do differently:

1. They pick fewer than 10 metrics that connect directly to their strategic priorities, not their industry averages.

2. They assign a single owner to each metric. When everyone owns a number, no one does.

3. They review KPIs weekly at the leadership level and ask one question: what decision does this number change for us right now?

Tracking everything feels responsible. It is not. It is a way of avoiding the harder work of deciding what actually matters.

What is the one metric your business could not afford to ignore this week, and who owns it?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Business.com rounded up 14 tools companies can use to track KPIs more effectively. The list is practical and worth a look if you are still managing performance data in spreadsheets.

But here is what the article does not address: for companies scaling past $50M, the tool is rarely the problem. The problem is that leadership teams have not agreed on which numbers actually reflect the health of the business versus which ones just look good in a board deck.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly. Companies invest in better dashboards and still make reactive decisions because the metrics feeding those dashboards were never properly chosen in the first place.

Before you upgrade your tracking tools, audit what you are tracking and why. That conversation will do more for your performance than any software.

Read the article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMingFBVV95cUxQcWNPSTVTUDVYYURoVkZKa0ItNEtQbmJqWlNJTlIzUVZqclAxMHFaajNobC1JbGNkZGZVajN6MWJLT1pJcXktVG10VG8zUUljdU43NU5WR1cyNDB4QkxONlJkb3hJR2FfNzdGZHd1VWhPbTktdU1vdTEzamFWY2ZFVDNKUFIwRG91ZDdWU1UyN2twNFpLd1JjU3EzTUpjdw?oc=5

post3.text:
Oracle NetSuite recently published a list of 30 financial metrics companies should consider tracking in 2026. It is a solid resource. It also illustrates a trap that chapter author Hector Arias and his co-authors Matt Radicelli and Jim Randall tackle head-on in Chapter 7 of our upcoming book.

The chapter is called Death by KPIs for a reason.

Scaling companies do not stall because they lack metrics. They stall because they have too many, tracked inconsistently, owned by no one, and disconnected from the decisions that actually move the business forward.

Chapter 7 gives leadership teams a clear method for cutting through the noise and building a performance measurement system that scales with them, not against them.

There is one diagnostic question in that chapter that will make most leadership teams uncomfortable. In the best way.

post1.text:
Most companies are failing at AI not because the technology is bad, but because leadership is lying to itself.

A recent Fortune survey found that 90% of executives admit AI has not meaningfully improved productivity. Yet many of those same leaders are trimming headcount on the assumption that it will. That is a dangerous bet.

Here is what scaling companies need to understand:

1. AI adoption without process redesign produces noise, not efficiency. The tool is only as good as the workflow it plugs into.

2. The gap between what executives believe is happening and what employees actually experience is where productivity goes to die. You cannot close that gap with a memo.

3. Leaders at the $50M to $500M stage cannot afford to treat AI as a checkbox. It has to be a deliberate operational decision with clear owners and measurable outcomes.

The companies winning with AI right now are not the ones moving fastest. They are the ones moving with intention.

What is your honest assessment of AI's impact on your team's output this year?

post2.text:
A recent piece in The New York Times surfaced a tension every scaling company should take seriously: CEOs believe their AI rollouts are succeeding. Their employees largely do not.

That disconnect is not just a morale problem. It is a strategy problem.

At Autobahn, we work with companies navigating the $50M to $500M growth stage, and this gap shows up constantly. Leaders invest in tools. Employees inherit confusion. No one owns the middle.

If your team cannot articulate how AI is making their specific job better, your rollout is not working, regardless of what the dashboard says.

Scaling companies need AI governance that lives at the operational level, not just the executive level. That starts with honest conversations, not announcements.

Read the full article here and ask yourself which side of this gap your company is on: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMivwFBVV95cUxQWWdVcmp6Vm8xaTlHbXhmRUp2bnU1Q2hlMUY1eG05ekVJSWFPRjRZWGcyODNDeUV4dW5IUndhM2NtWlJDSE1QSmhlekNNVUotb2NHRjBwRTc4dkR0Y3RNeUIwWlZNUk1hOTc2dEJYTEVUUlVhSXFmeUx1RlZWNjJ0ZmhINTRHcXZac0NtOUd2RE9oTUU1Rk9TLWJmSlpFTWxfaVlSdUhkZ2p3ZVB3LXhWSVZSS004ZkNzRlFWUzVjVQ?oc=5

post3.text:
Bloomberg recently gathered AI productivity insights from a dozen CEOs. The strategies were practical. The underlying challenge, though, was the same one we see in every scaling company: figuring out where AI actually fits into the way your business runs day to day.

That question sits at the center of Chapter 8 in our upcoming book, Rock Your Business. The chapter is called The Third Monitor Theory, written by Hudson Shank and Jonathan Slain, and it offers a concrete way to think about how leaders at growing companies should position AI inside their existing operations, not as an add-on, but as an integrated layer of decision support.

The insight is simpler than most AI frameworks you have seen. And that is exactly the point.

post1.text:
The leaders most qualified to run a $50M+ company are often the ones most convinced they don't belong there.

Imposter syndrome isn't a sign of weakness. It's a byproduct of genuine self-awareness. Leaders who feel it are usually the ones paying close enough attention to know what they don't know. That's not a liability. That's a competitive advantage, if you know how to use it.

Forbes recently reported that women who dominate the travel industry still report widespread feelings of not deserving their seat at the table. These aren't underperformers. They're industry leaders. The feeling and the reality have almost nothing to do with each other.

Here's what that means for scaling companies:

First, imposter syndrome often signals that a leader is operating at the edge of their current capability, which is exactly where growth happens. Second, leaders who never question themselves tend to stop learning. Third, the goal isn't to eliminate the feeling. It's to stop letting it make decisions for you.

So ask yourself: Is self-doubt slowing you down, or is it keeping you sharp?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Campaign US makes a point that most leadership coaching gets completely wrong: don't try to eliminate imposter syndrome. Put it to work.

That reframe matters enormously for companies scaling past $50M. At that stage, leaders are constantly being asked to operate in territory they haven't navigated before. The ones who mistake self-doubt for incompetence stall. The ones who treat it as a signal that they're in the right stretch assignment keep moving.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern repeatedly. The psychological game of leadership is just as important as the operational one, and it's the piece most growth-stage companies neglect entirely.

If this topic is on your radar, the full article is worth your time.

Chapter 9 of Rock Your Business is titled "How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It?" and it asks a question most leaders at the $50M to $500M stage are quietly asking themselves.

Authored by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo, the chapter takes a direct look at imposter syndrome not as a personal flaw to fix, but as a psychological pattern that shows up specifically because a leader is growing faster than their self-concept has caught up.

One thing the chapter makes clear: the leaders who scale successfully are rarely the most confident ones in the room. They're the ones who have learned what to do with the doubt.

There's a framework inside that changes how you read your own internal resistance. We'll leave it at that for now.

post1.text:
Most founders treat life planning like a retirement activity. That is a mistake that costs them everything that matters.

A recent Deutsche Bank Wealth Management analysis on entrepreneur wealth planning makes something clear: the financial decisions you delay while scaling are the hardest to reverse later. Life planning is not what you do after you build the company. It is a core operating discipline while you are building it.

Here is what leaders scaling past $50M consistently get wrong:

1. They optimize the business for exit value without deciding what they actually want life to look like after the exit. The result is a great number and a hollow next chapter.

2. They treat personal financial planning as separate from business strategy. At this scale, they are the same conversation.

3. They assume more revenue solves the design problem. It does not. It just funds the wrong life faster.

The companies that scale well and the people inside them that stay whole are the ones who plan both trajectories at once.

What does your business currently optimize for that your life has never agreed to?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Entrepreneur reveals something worth sitting with: roughly three out of four founders regret selling their business within a year of closing the deal. Not because the terms were bad. Because they had no plan for what came next.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern in companies scaling from $50M to $500M all the time. Leaders pour everything into building enterprise value and nothing into designing the life that is supposed to follow.

The exit is not the finish line. It is a transition. And transitions without intention tend to feel like loss, regardless of the dollar amount on the wire.

If you are scaling right now, start the life design conversation today, not the quarter before you close.

Read the full piece here: https://news.google.

post3.text:
Data showing that most founders regret selling within a year is not a negotiation problem. It is a life design problem.

Chapter 10 of Rock Your Business, titled Coming Up for Air, addresses exactly this. Written by Samantha Frost and Jonathan and Katherine Slain, the chapter makes a case that most leaders at the $50M to $500M stage never hear until it is too late: scaling a business and designing a life have to happen on the same timeline.

One insight the chapter surfaces is that the feeling of regret after an exit rarely traces back to the deal itself. It traces back to decisions that were never made about identity, purpose, and structure outside the company.

If you are building something significant, this chapter will challenge how you think about what you are actually building toward.
